A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same scaling-law meta-analysis. Their text, equations, figures, references, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original empirical analyses of collected model-training data, including fitted scaling laws, prediction errors, checkpoint-selection experiments, and cross-validation analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those original empirical analyses and adds Huber-loss results in Appendix E and Figure 9.

M1.justification: The main five-parameter scaling-law workflow remains. Equation 1 introduces exponentiated coefficients, but the PDFs do not establish whether this corrects the earlier description or changes the implementation. Section 3.2 discusses Huber loss as a fitting alternative, whereas Appendix E describes replacing ARE, leaving uncertainty about whether the estimation objective changed.

E1.justification: Both versions use the collection of 485 pretrained models, more than 40 scaled families, and 1.9 million evaluated training steps for loss-extrapolation analyses. The Huber analysis uses existing model families. Newly discussed BabyLM and DoVE resources are related work, not added evaluation datasets.

E2.justification: Section 5.2 retains the best-performance and highest-training-compute baselines with the same definitions and comparisons. L-BFGS was already considered in v1. The Huber appendix presents a supplementary replication rather than adding a baseline to those comparisons.

E3.justification: Appendix E introduces a Huber-based analysis and specifies its threshold, although its role in fitting versus evaluation is inconsistently described. Figure 7 changes the reported representative model configurations, including GPT-3 175B to 13B. The main held-out-largest-model and ARE evaluation design remains.

E4.justification: New Appendix E and Figure 9 test whether the main trends persist under Huber loss for GPT-3, Pythia, GPT-2, and Llama. Figure 7 revises the illustrative trajectory cases. Existing checkpoint, model-size, model-count, downward-extrapolation, and cross-validation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version supplies experimental replicate counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the scaling-law comparisons. Seed-variability discussions remain unchanged. The added description of L-BFGS retries does not introduce statistical uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Figure 9 adds Huber-loss results reported to show similar overall trends. Figure 7 replaces several trajectory and prediction examples with different model configurations, so their changed losses are not same-setting performance gains. Main findings such as 18% average baseline ARE and 99.49% variance explained by three principal components remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation 1 changes the stated coefficients from E, A, and B to e^E, e^A, and e^B, explicitly encoding and explaining coefficient positivity that v1 did not specify. This is a limited revision of the formal model specification; no new theorems or proofs are introduced.

C1.justification: The central contributions and conclusions remain: the collected dataset, benefits of intermediate checkpoints, tradeoffs between model size and number, cross-family parameter transfer, and potentially fewer effective scaling-law parameters. The new practical-recommendations table consolidates existing takeaways.

C2.justification: Sections 2 and 6 more explicitly qualify that partially trained and converged models can differ because of learning-rate schedules, with their usefulness requiring empirical assessment. Section 5.1 reframes partial training as an alternative to scaling layer counts. The main limitations concerning ARE and aggregation across families remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds details about L-BFGS convergence failures, slowness, and required retries, and documents the Huber threshold in Appendix E. It also explains how architectural dimensions co-vary with parameter count. Code and data access still point to the same repository.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of BabyLM 2025, DoVE, and Maia Polo et al.'s SLOTH work, plus a second BabyLM challenge citation. The new resource discussion and connections to cross-family prediction modestly expand research positioning without changing the paper's central contribution.

P1.justification: v2 tightens introductory and explanatory passages, shortens several question headings, and simplifies family notation. It adds a practical summary, Impact Statement, and acknowledgments while preserving the main twelve-section narrative and existing appendix organization.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout and moves the conceptual diagram forward, changing v1 Figure 2 into v2 Figure 1. It adds a recommendations table and Figure 9. Figure 6 removes numerical cell annotations and changes the color range from 0–100 to 0–35; Figure 7 substantially redesigns the trajectory displays and prediction annotations.

improvement.justification: v2 modestly improves clarity and usability through the explicit positivity specification, clearer representative trajectory plots, and practical-recommendations table. Appendix E adds limited sensitivity evidence, although Huber's fitting-versus-evaluation role remains unclear and Figure 6 loses exact numerical annotations. These benefits are useful but leave the central evidence and main limitations largely unchanged.
